plain: A few simple techniques make a big visual difference. Sand progressively through finer grits (start around 120, work up to 220 or 320) rather than jumping straight to a fine grit, since skipping steps leaves visible scratches even after a fine sanding. Raise the grain by lightly wetting the wood, letting it dry, then sanding again, which prevents a fuzzy texture once finish is applied. Use a sharp carving tool and take light, controlled cuts rather than forcing deep ones, since clean tool marks look far more intentional than ragged ones. Finally, apply a finish like danish oil, wax, or a thin coat of polyurethane, which deepens the wood's color and gives it the smooth sheen associated with professional work.

plain: Marburg virus disease was first identified in 1967, when simultaneous outbreaks occurred in Marburg and Frankfurt, Germany, as well as Belgrade, in what was then Yugoslavia. The outbreaks were traced to African green monkeys imported from Uganda for laboratory research and vaccine production, and laboratory workers who handled the infected animals' tissues became the first documented human cases. In total, 31 people were infected and 7 died in that initial outbreak. The virus was later found to be a filovirus closely related to Ebola, and its natural reservoir is now believed to be the Egyptian fruit bat.
